newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Croat camp chief helped prisoners - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croat camp chief helped prisoners - lawyer.

text.p: A Bosnian Croat accused of atrocities against Serbs at the Celebici prison camp in 1992 protected detainees from beatings by guards and helped others to get out, his lawyer told a U.N. warcrimes tribunal on Tuesday.

Zdravko "Pavo" Mucic is charged along with Moslems Hazim Delic, Esad Landzo and Zejnil Delalic with war crimes allegedly committed at the camp in central Bosnia. Mucic, 41, was the camp commander. All four claim to be innocent.
"You will hear witnesses say that whenever Pavo was in the camp, there were no serious beatings," defence lawyer Branislav Tapuskovic said in his opening remarks to the Hague court.
"He went to fetch medicine for detainees...He did everything so that prisoners could leave the camp as soon as possible."
"You will hear people say 'Pavo protected me'."
Tapuskovic stressed he was only defending Mucic, but this is a joint trial with four co-accused in the dock.
Mucic, dressed in a grey sweatshirt and flanked by armed U.N. guards, looked relaxed, taking notes and occasionally smiling and chatting to Landzo sitting next to him.

Mucic and Delalic, a 48-year-old former Bosnian Moslem military leader, are accused of command responsibility for atrocities at the camp, including at least 14 murders and a grisly catalogue of torture, rape and sexual assault.
Deputy camp commander Delic, 32, is also charged with command responsibility and, along with 24-year-old camp guard Landzo, of taking part in torture, rapes and killings.
They are charged with beating elderly men to death with wooden planks, baseball bats, shovels and cable and torturing inmates with pliers, acid, electric shock and hot metal pincers.
In Tuesday's afternoon session, Cynthia White McMurrey, Landzo's defence lawyer, urged a separate trial for Mucic.
She said that after morning comments from Tapuskovic, there was now a "visible" conflict of interest between Mucic's line of defence and that of the three Moslems.
But presiding judge Adolphus Karibi-Whyte from Nigeria dismissed her claim, saying the court had already considered motions on separate trials and ruled against them.

The prosecution then called its first expert witness -- Ton Beelen, a Dutch police forensic investigator sent by the tribunal to Celebici in October last year to take photographs, video footage and measurements of the camp.

The court was shown a series of some 60 photographs of the inside and outside of the camp's white concrete buildings -- now used by the Bosnian army to store oil products. Some of the buildings still had bullet holes in them.
The accused showed signs of recognition as the photographs and video footage were displayed on courtroom monitors.
Mucic and Landzo continued to take notes, at times seeming to disagree with descriptions of the images given by Deelen, prompting them to pass pieces of paper forward to their lawyers.
Delic sat impassively, mostly staring straight ahead, chewing gum. Delalic looked tired, rubbing his eyes and yawning.
The prosecution said its next step would be to call two former Celebici detainees as witnesses, primarily to show the general conditions of prisoners at the camp.
The trial is a watershed for the Hague-based tribunal, set up in 1993 by the United Nations Security Council to punish war crimes committed during the bitter 3-1/2 year Bosnian conflict.
The first group trial, it is also the first to focus on atrocities against Serbs and the first in which command responsibility for war crimes is considered.
Accused of anti-Serb bias, the tribunal has stated that its war crimes investigations are carried out irrespective of political or ethnic background.
Most of the 74 men it has so far charged are Serbs. Only seven suspects are actually in the tribunal's custody.
